When traders look for a reliable platform to analyze markets, place orders, and share ideas, the debate often comes down to **[TradingView](https://in.tradingview.com/?aff_id=167054) vs Thinkorswim**. Both tools enjoy strong followings, but they cater to slightly different workflows and preferences. This guide walks you through the most important aspects—features, pricing, usability, and ideal user profiles—so you can decide which platform fits your trading style best.

## Platform Overview  

### TradingView Basics  
TradingView started as a web‑based charting service and has grown into a full‑featured trading ecosystem. Its hallmark is the intuitive, HTML5 chart interface that works in any browser, plus desktop and mobile apps. Users love the vast library of community‑created indicators, the ability to publish trading ideas, and the seamless integration with dozens of brokers for order execution. While the core charting is free, advanced tools like multiple chart layouts, deeper backtesting, and premium data require a paid subscription.

### Thinkorswim Basics  
Thinkorswim (often abbreviated TOS) is the flagship platform of TD Ameritrade, now part of Charles Schwab. It is a downloadable desktop application renowned for its powerful analytical tools, thinkScript programming language, and paper trading environment. Thinkorswim shines for active traders who need advanced order types, complex options analytics, and institutional‑grade data feeds. Because it’s tied to a brokerage account, you get direct market access without extra fees, but the platform has a steeper learning curve and is less social‑oriented than TradingView.

## Key Features Comparison  

### Charting Tools  
TradingView excels at visual clarity. Its charts are highly customizable, with over 100 built‑in studies, drawing tools, and the ability to layer multiple time‑frames on a single screen. The platform also supports pine script, letting users create custom indicators and strategies that run directly in the browser. Thinkorswim offers equally robust charting, but the interface feels denser. Its thinkScript language is more powerful for complex backtesting and strategy development, yet it requires installing the desktop client and a bit more coding know‑how.

### Order Types & Execution  
If you need to route trades directly from the chart, TradingView integrates with a growing list of brokers (e.g., OANDA, Forex.com, Tradestation) through its broker‑connect feature. Order types include market, limit, stop, and conditional orders, though advanced bracket or OCO orders depend on the broker’s capabilities. Thinkorswim, being a broker‑native platform, provides direct access to equity, options, futures, and Forex markets with a full suite of order types—including OCO, trailing stops, and complex multi‑leg options strategies—executed instantly via Schwab’s infrastructure.

### Community & Social Features  
One of TradingView’s biggest draws is its social network. Users can publish trading ideas, follow other traders, comment on charts, and even copy strategies via the “Ideas” feed. This community aspect fosters learning and idea generation, especially for newer traders. Thinkorswim lacks a built‑in social feed; its community is more fragmented across forums, chat rooms, and third‑party sites. While you can share thinkScript scripts, the platform does not emphasize public idea sharing as a core feature.

## Pricing & Plans  

### Free vs Paid  
TradingView offers a free tier that includes basic charts, one indicator per chart, and limited saved layouts. The three paid plans—Pro ($14.95/mo), Pro+ ($29.95/mo), and Premium ($59.95/mo)—unlock multiple charts per layout, more indicators, priority data, and extended backtesting. Thinkorswim is free to use if you have a funded Schwab account; there are no subscription fees for the platform itself. However, you may incur broker‑specific costs such as commissions, fees, or data subscriptions depending on the assets you trade.

### Thinkorswim Costs  
Because Thinkorswim is broker‑linked, the primary cost comes from your trading activity. Schwab eliminated commissions on online stock and ETF trades, and options trades carry a $0.65 per contract fee (plus exchange fees). Futures and Forex have their own fee structures. If you only need the platform for paper trading or analysis, you can open a Schwab account with zero minimum deposit and use Thinkorswim at no extra cost beyond any market data subscriptions you might add.
